x: All three are correct: polar seas have only a single cold layer, in mid-latitudes the warm surface layer forms only in summer, and the tropical thermocline (about 500-1,000 m) is where temperature drops fast with depth.

Humboldt (South Pacific, Peru-Chile) and Benguela (South Atlantic, Namibia) are both cold currents. Agulhas, Brazil, Kuroshio, Florida, Mozambique and Norwegian are all warm, so options A, B and C contain no cold current.

A giant Pavona clavus (potato patch coral) colony was reported near Kadmat Island, Lakshadweep. Options A and C mismatch Pavona clavus and PMMSY, and B wrongly pairs D-COIN with the oil sardine fishery.
El Nino recurs about every 3-7 years. Some 2026 notes give a wider 2-7-year range, but 3-7 years is the standard figure; 1-2, 8-12 and 15-20 years are wrong.

The annual range of ocean temperature is smaller in the vast Pacific than in the Atlantic: a larger, more extensive body of water heats and cools more slowly, so its temperature varies less over the year.

In the tropics the western sides of oceans are warmer, but in temperate latitudes the westerlies reverse this and make the eastern sections warmer, as the North Atlantic Drift does off NW Europe. Humboldt, Labrador and Benguela are cold currents.

Tropical oceans have a warm surface layer to about 500 m (20-25 degC), a thermocline from about 500-1,000 m where temperature falls fast, and a cold deep layer near 0-4 degC. A, B and D misplace or omit these layers.
